summary: This informational document discusses options and requirements for rendering RFCs as PDF, as outlined in RFC 6949. It also covers the use of PDF for Internet-Drafts and the software tools available or needed for producing and working with PDF.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7995 recommends how to make PDF versions of RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It covers print layout and features that help people and software read, search, preserve, and access the documents.

subtitle: Recommendations for making RFC PDFs readable, searchable, accessible, and suitable for preservation.

tldr.problem: PDF files can look alike while differing in whether their text can be searched, read by assistive tools, or preserved with source material.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends PDF 1.7, PDF/A-3 level U for RFCs, PDF/UA for accessibility, and rules for page layout, text order, metadata, links, and embedded files.
tldr.outcome: It records recommendations for RFC and Internet-Draft PDF production. The unit metadata says RFC 7995 is updated by RFC 9920.

today: RFC 7995 is an Informational document and is updated by RFC 9920. It records PDF recommendations whose details were expected to change as publication tools were completed.

sections.title: Why PDF Production Needs Rules
sections.content:
Future RFCs use XML as their source and can be rendered in several formats, including PDF. PDF offers many options, so files that look alike can differ in whether they contain real text, links, embedded fonts, or digital signatures.

This memo discusses PDF choices for RFCs and Internet-Drafts. It says the recommendations may change as publication tools are completed, and later changes may not be backward compatible.
sections.plainLanguage: A PDF can contain real text or only a picture of text, even when both look the same. This memo recommends PDF features that make RFCs easier to use and preserve.

sections.title: PDF Versions and Conformance Standards
sections.content:
The memo recommends PDF 1.7 because widely available viewers support it. It recommends PDF/A-3 with conformance level U for RFCs; this profile supports preservation and requires Unicode mapping.

PDF/A-3 can carry extra files, including the XML source. The memo recommends PDF/UA for accessibility, so the PDF requirements cover both long-term use and access by readers.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC PDFs should use PDF 1.7 and meet PDF/A-3 level U. The memo also recommends PDF/UA so people using accessibility tools can use the document.

sections.title: Page Layout, Fonts, and Links
sections.content:
The memo recommends A4 portrait pages by default, with left and right margins of 20 mm and top and bottom margins of 33 mm. This layout is intended to print on A4 and US Letter without scaling. Headers and footers should be unobtrusive and should not interfere with screen readers.

All fonts should be embedded. Hyperlinks available in the HTML version should remain active in the PDF, including links in the table of contents. The PDF should resemble the HTML version in spirit, while allowing print-specific typefaces and page numbers.
sections.plainLanguage: Use the specified A4 page and margin settings so the document can also print on US Letter without scaling. Embed fonts and keep the document's links active.

sections.title: Text, Metadata, and Embedded Source
sections.content:
The PDF should preserve the full text from the XML and arrange its internal text in the same logical order. This supports searching, annotation, and text-to-speech. The memo also recommends Unicode mappings for text and the use of SVG when both SVG and ASCII artwork are available.

Alt-text for figures should be stored in the PDF, and XML metadata should be embedded as XMP. For RFCs, the PDF should include the XML source and illustrations; named source-code entries and bitmap images should also be embedded.
sections.plainLanguage: The PDF should store text in reading order, with descriptions for images and information about the document. It should also carry the XML source and illustrations.

sections.title: Signatures and PDF Security
sections.content:
A digital signature can help show that an RFC is original and unmodified. The memo suggests signing PDFs produced by RFC Editor tools and describes restrictions for later changes, but leaves the signing method to a separate policy.

Submitted PDFs could contain malware targeting readers, printers, or validation tools. The production toolset could also be exploited to create harmful files. The memo recommends careful security review of production tools and careful examination of submitted PDFs.
sections.plainLanguage: A signature can help verify that a PDF has not changed. Because a PDF or its production tools may be unsafe, the memo recommends checking both carefully.
